# Summary

"Social sciencey" regressions. We compute join counts at the level
of individual languages under various operationalizations of
geographical neighbourhood.

We'll need the following packages:

```{r}
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggsci)
library(tidyverse)
```


# Hyperparameters

Set global values for these (used in everything that follows
unless otherwise specified):

```{r}
GREX <- 1.0   # gravity exponent
CAP <- 50     # include only the CAP nearest neighbours
```


# Join "counts" (better: 'join scores'?)

For a given type and a given language $L$, the join score with respect
to neighbouring languages carrying a type of the OR kind (i.e.
neighbour shares at least one feature value with the focal language)
is defined as
$$
J = \sum_{L'} w_{LL'}
$$
where $L'$ ranges over the focal's OR neighbours and $w_{LL'}$, the
_weight_ of the join between $L$ and $L'$, is taken to be either
$$
w_{LL'} = d(L,L')^{-s}
$$
where $d(L,L')$ is the great-circle distance between $L$ and $L'$ and
$s$ is a parameter, the _gravity exponent_, or
$$
w_{LL'} = r(L')^{-s}
$$
where $r(L')$ is the rank of $L'$ among the neighbours of $L$ (i.e. $L'$
is the $r(L')$th nearest neighbour of $L$).

The first option gives us kilometre-based neighbourhoods, the second,
rank-based neighbourhoods.

We have good theoretical reasons for believing that the gravity
exponent $s$ ought to have a value very close to $1$. Setting $s=0$
recovers plain join counts. Setting $s=2$ would give us the inverse
square law---something we no longer really believe to be sensible.


# The data

The join counts are calculated by a Julia script (`jclang.jl`).
We now read these results into R.

```{r}
wals <- read.csv("../longresults/newjoins_wals.csv")
wals$dataset <- "WALS"

gram <- read.csv("../longresults/newjoins_grambank.csv")
gram$dataset <- "Grambank"

data <- rbind(wals, gram)
data$type <- factor(data$type)
```

This is the structure of the dataframe.

```{r}
head(data)
```

Each row corresponds to a type in one language. The meanings of the columns:

- pair: feature pair i.e. typology
- class: whether the pair is a target (word-order) or control pair
- status: whether the pair is interacting or non-interacting. This decision is based on Jäger's new stuff. A pair is taken to be interacting if its logarithmic Bayes factor is at least 4. Control pairs are taken to be non-interacting by fiat.
- type: for instance, if pair is "VS & VO", then the type "12" would refer to VS paired with OV
- attestation: whether the type is overattested, underattested or neither, as established by the statistical test described in our manuscript
- pedigree: either "dispreferred" (type is an underattested type in an interacting pair), "control under" (type is an underattested type in a control pair) or "other" (type is something else)
- Language_ID: language
- Family: language's family
- degree: cap on the size of neighbourhood. We only look at languages up to the 'degree'th nearest neighbour. Here, this is either 10, 50, 100 or 500.
- gravity_exponent: see explanation above
- gravity_type: either "km" or "rank"
- min_distance: the minimum distance across all joins for this particular type and this particular language
- mean_distance: the mean distance across all joins for this particular type and this particular language
- max_distance: the max distance across all joins for this particular type and this particular language
- frequency: frequency of the type
- joincount: join count/score for the type and language
- dataset: "WALS" or "Grambank"


# First results: WALS

First, we'll look at two subsets of this dataframe. One assumes kilometre
neighbourhoods, the other, rank neighbourhoods.

```{r}
data_km = subset(data, 
                 degree == CAP & 
                   gravity_exponent == GREX & 
                   gravity_type == "km" & 
                   pedigree %in% c("dispreferred", "control under"))

data_rank = subset(data, 
                   degree == CAP & 
                     gravity_exponent == GREX & 
                     gravity_type == "rank" & 
                     pedigree %in% c("dispreferred", "control under"))
```

A basic regression will have `joincount` as the dependent variable,
`Language_ID`, `Family` and `type` as random effects,^[I haven't added Macroarea yet, as that information would have to be fetched from another file and merged, and I couldn't be bothered to do this yet. But we can add it later, if desired.] `frequency` as a main
effect, and possibly `pedigree` as a main effect (depending on whether
we're looking at the null model---no pedigree---or the alternative
model---pedigree included).

First, km-based neighbourhoods in WALS:

```{r}
mod <- lmer(joincount ~ (1 | Language_ID) + 
            (1 | Family) + 
            (1 | type) + 
            frequency + 
            pedigree, subset(data_km, dataset == "WALS"))

summary(mod)
```

Null model:

```{r}
mod_null <- lmer(joincount ~ (1 | Language_ID) + 
                 (1 | Family) + 
                 (1 | type) + 
                 frequency, subset(data_km, dataset == "WALS"))

summary(mod_null)
```

Comparison of AIC:

```{r}
AIC(mod)
```

```{r}
AIC(mod_null)
```

This suggests that pedigree is an important predictor. Furthermore,
in the alternative model, pedigree has a positive coefficient
with "control under" as the reference level, meaning that dispreferred
types have higher join counts than control underattested types
(even when controlled for frequency, language, family and type).
Nice!

With rank-based neighbourhoods:

```{r}
mod <- lmer(joincount ~ (1 | Language_ID) + 
            (1 | Family) + 
            (1 | type) + 
            frequency + 
            pedigree, subset(data_rank, dataset == "WALS"))

summary(mod)
```

Null model:

```{r}
mod_null <- lmer(joincount ~ (1 | Language_ID) + 
                 (1 | Family) + 
                 (1 | type) + 
                 frequency, subset(data_rank, dataset == "WALS"))

summary(mod_null)
```

Comparison of AIC:

```{r}
AIC(mod)
```

```{r}
AIC(mod_null)
```

Same thing.


# First results: Grambank

In Grambank, there is a slight complication: there are languages
with neighbours at a zero kilometres distance. This crashes the
km-based gravity model as it invites division by zero. To avoid
the problem, I've replaced all zero distances with 10 km for now.

## km-based

```{r}
mod <- lmer(joincount ~ 
            (1 | type) +
            (1 | Language_ID) + 
            (1 | Family) + 
            frequency + 
            pedigree, subset(data_km, dataset == "Grambank"))

summary(mod)
```

Null model:

```{r}
mod_null <- lmer(joincount ~ 
                 (1 | type) +
                 (1 | Language_ID) + 
                 (1 | Family) + 
                 frequency, subset(data_km, dataset == "Grambank"))

summary(mod_null)
```

Comparison of AIC:

```{r}
AIC(mod)
```

```{r}
AIC(mod_null)
```

## rank-based

```{r}
mod <- lmer(joincount ~ 
            (1 | type) +
            (1 | Language_ID) + 
            (1 | Family) + 
            frequency + 
            pedigree, subset(data_rank, dataset == "Grambank"))

summary(mod)
```

Null model:

```{r}
mod_null <- lmer(joincount ~ 
                 (1 | type) +
                 (1 | Language_ID) + 
                 (1 | Family) + 
                 frequency, subset(data_rank, dataset == "Grambank"))

summary(mod_null)
```

Comparison of AIC:

```{r}
AIC(mod)
```

```{r}
AIC(mod_null)
```




# Visualization: WALS

The plot Ricardo wanted to see:

```{r}
source("dumbbell.R")
```

Using km-based neighbourhoods:

```{r}
p <- dumbbell_plot(subset(data_km, dataset == "WALS"))
p <- p + ggtitle("WALS, km-based")
print(p)
```

Using rank-based neighbourhoods:

```{r}
p <- dumbbell_plot(subset(data_rank, dataset == "WALS"))
p <- p + ggtitle("WALS, rank-based")
print(p)
```

This looks very nice---whenever both pedigrees are present in a frequency
bin, the dispreferred dot is higher.

# Lower gravity exponent for km-based model

Try a value of $0.1$ for the gravity exponent:

```{r}
data_km = subset(data, 
                 degree == CAP & 
                   gravity_exponent == 0.1 & 
                   gravity_type == "km" & 
                   pedigree %in% c("dispreferred", "control under"))
```


# Preferred versus control overattested types

This began as a sanity check---we expected not to see an effect
between preferred and contol overattested types. But in fact we do:

```{r}
data_sanity_km = subset(data, 
                        degree == CAP & 
                          gravity_exponent == GREX & 
                          gravity_type == "km" & 
                          pedigree %in% c("preferred", "control over"))

data_sanity_rank = subset(data, 
                          degree == CAP & 
                            gravity_exponent == GREX & 
                            gravity_type == "rank" & 
                            pedigree %in% c("preferred", "control over"))
```

## WALS

```{r}
p <- dumbbell_plot(subset(data_sanity_rank, dataset == "WALS"))
p <- p + ggtitle("WALS, rank-based")
print(p)
```

Regression:

```{r}
mod <- lmer(joincount ~ (1 | Language_ID) + 
            (1 | Family) + 
            (1 | type) + 
            frequency + 
            pedigree, subset(data_sanity_rank, dataset == "WALS"))

summary(mod)
```

Null model:

```{r}
mod_null <- lmer(joincount ~ (1 | Language_ID) + 
                 (1 | Family) + 
                 (1 | type) + 
                 frequency, subset(data_sanity_rank, dataset == "WALS"))

summary(mod_null)
```

Comparison of AIC:

```{r}
AIC(mod)
```

```{r}
AIC(mod_null)
```


## Grambank

```{r}
p <- dumbbell_plot(subset(data_sanity_rank, dataset == "Grambank"))
p <- p + ggtitle("Grambank, rank-based")
print(p)
```

Regression:

```{r}
mod <- lmer(joincount ~ (1 | Language_ID) + 
            (1 | Family) + 
            (1 | type) + 
            frequency +
```
